## References

1. [Establishing Best Practices for Building Rigorous Agentic Benchmarks (Zhu et al., 2025)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.02825)
2. Code: [uiuc-kang-lab/agentic-benchmarks @ ae11247](https://github.com/uiuc-kang-lab/agentic-benchmarks)

# Notes

## The problem: agent leaderboards report numbers nobody checked

When a lab announces that its model resolves 35% of τ-bench-Airline tasks or tops SWE-bench-Verified, people treat that number as a measurement of capability. This paper asks a blunt question: does the number actually measure what it claims? The answer for many popular agentic benchmarks is "not reliably". The headline example is striking. On τ-bench-Airline, an agent that does nothing at all scores 38%, which beats a GPT-4o-based agent (35%). On SWE-Lancer, an agent that never touches the task can score 100% by overwriting the test files. These are not corner cases of obscure benchmarks. The authors picked benchmarks that OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, DeepSeek and others cite in their model launch posts.

Why is this more of a problem for agent benchmarks than for older ones? A multiple-choice benchmark like MMLU has a closed answer set: the model picks A, B, C or D and you compare it to a label. There is almost nothing to get wrong in the grader. An agentic benchmark instead hands the agent an environment (a sandbox, a database, a website), a set of tools, and a goal. The agent then acts for many steps and produces an open-ended outcome: a code patch, a changed database, a free-text answer. Someone has to write a program that decides whether that outcome counts as success. That grading program is itself software, written under deadline, and it inherits every bug and blind spot software has. The paper's contribution is to name the ways this goes wrong, turn them into a checklist (the Agentic Benchmark Checklist, ABC), and show with experiments how big the resulting errors are.

This connects directly to [[measurement-correction-inflates-apparent-agent-progress]] and [[eval-precision-vs-eval-validity]]: precise numbers (tight error bars) mean nothing if the grader is measuring the wrong thing.

## The core idea: two links in a chain

The paper's conceptual frame (Figure 1) is a chain with three nodes and two links:

target capability → task success → positive evaluation result.

The benchmark designer wants to measure a *target capability*, for example "can the agent follow airline refund policy". They design a task whose *success* should require that capability. Then they write a grader that outputs a *positive result* when the task succeeded. A score is trustworthy only if both links are equivalences, meaning each side implies the other.

**Task validity** is the first link. The paper defines it as: "a task should be solvable if and only if the agent possesses the target capability." "If and only if" has two directions, and each direction has its own failure mode. If an agent *without* the capability can still succeed, the task has a **shortcut**, which produces false positives (overestimation). If an agent *with* the capability cannot succeed, the task is **impossible**, which produces false negatives (underestimation). A do-nothing agent passing τ-bench is a shortcut. OSWorld tasks broken because a live website changed its HTML are impossible tasks.

**Outcome validity** is the second link: the grader's verdict must truly indicate task success. SWE-bench-Verified breaks this link because its unit tests are incomplete, so a wrong patch can pass them.

The distinction matters because the fixes differ. Task-validity bugs live in the environment and task setup (leaked answers, stale websites, tasks with empty ground truth). Outcome-validity bugs live in the grading method (weak tests, loose string matching, unvalidated LLM judges). Separating them tells a benchmark builder where to look.

The paper identifies two reasons agentic benchmarks make both links hard to hold. First, **complex task setup**: beyond a prompt, there is an environment and tools, and each is a place for leaks, drift, and state bugs. Second, **unstructured task outcomes**: grading a code patch or a changed database has no single canonical answer, so graders use proxies (tests, substrings, state hashes) that can be gamed or be too strict.

## How the checklist was built

The authors started from 78 benchmarks cited by major AI providers between January 2024 and March 2025 (plus award-winning academic benchmarks), filtered to 25 agentic ones (Table 2), and then to a study corpus of 17 (Table 3). To count as agentic, a benchmark had to require multistep reasoning or command execution, which excludes SimpleQA, MMLU, HumanEval and MBPP. They then combined four sources to draft the checks: their own benchmark-building experience (the lab built CVE-Bench), best practices already present in some benchmarks, published bug reports about specific benchmarks, and established techniques from software testing. Appendix C traces every check back to its source, which is useful: most checks come from a real, documented failure rather than from speculation.

Finally they applied ABC to ten open-source benchmarks chosen to cover every capability type and evaluation method (Table 1): SWE-bench, SWE-Lancer, KernelBench, BIRD, Cybench, MLE-bench, GAIA, τ-bench, WebArena and OSWorld. Scoring is simple: each applicable check gets 1 if satisfied and 0 otherwise, and each section's score is the average of its applicable items. For every issue they found, they designed an experiment to measure its effect on reported performance.

## The checklist itself

ABC has three parts. I will explain each group of checks by the failure it prevents, because the checks only make sense once you see the bug behind them.

### Task validity (T.1–T.10)

**Tools (T.1–T.3).** If the prompt does not say which Python or package version is installed (T.1), an agent may write correct code for the wrong version and fail. If a task depends on an external API, that API must stay reachable and within rate limits (T.2), and if it goes down the harness should stop or flag the run rather than silently scoring failures (T.3). WebArena's self-hosted websites hitting rate limits is the cited example: agents failed for reasons that had nothing to do with their skill.

**Environment (T.4–T.6).** Leftover state from one task must be wiped before the next (T.4). The vivid example is KernelBench, which ran the ground-truth kernel before the agent's kernel on the same GPU and did not clear memory, so an agent's kernel could read the correct answer out of leftover GPU memory through an out-of-bounds read. The agent must be isolated from any ground-truth information (T.5), which is exactly what SWE-Lancer violates. And the environment must be frozen at release (T.6): no live websites, because live websites change.

**Implementation (T.7–T.10).** Ground-truth labels must be verified (T.7) and each task confirmed solvable (T.8). An **oracle solver** (T.9) is a program that automatically solves every task using privileged knowledge. It is a cheap, powerful sanity check: if the oracle cannot pass a task, the task or grader is broken. Finally the implementation must be free of exploitable vulnerabilities (T.10). The practical advice here is to inspect outliers in pilot runs: "if agents consistently fail on easy tasks, this may indicate that tasks are impossible, whereas if agents only succeed on difficult tasks, it may indicate shortcuts." This is the same instinct as [[transcript-spotting-heuristics-for-reward-hacking]], applied by the benchmark builder instead of the model trainer.

### Outcome validity (O.a–O.i)

These checks are grouped by what kind of outcome is graded and by which grading method.

**Information acquisition** (the agent returns a text answer):

- *Whole-string matching* compares the whole answer to the label. It must accept semantically equivalent phrasings (O.a.1, "63 min" vs "1 hour 3 minutes") and tolerate filler words (O.a.2).
- *Substring matching* passes if the label appears somewhere in the answer. This is more forgiving, which opens three holes. Negation: "the answer is not Paris" contains "Paris" (O.b.1). Enumeration: an agent that lists every candidate answer contains the right one (O.b.2). Guessing: if the label is "4" or empty, it is trivially contained (O.b.3).
- *LLM-as-a-judge* uses a model to grade the answer. The judge's accuracy, self-consistency and agreement with humans must be measured, not assumed (O.c.1), and it must resist adversarial inputs (O.c.2). See [[llm-as-judge-evaluation-pattern]], [[2306.05685 - Judging LLM-as-a-Judge (MT-Bench)]] and [[2511.21140 - How to Correctly Report LLM-as-a-Judge Evaluations]].

**Code generation** (the agent writes code):

- *Unit tests* check individual functions. Tests must be human-verified (O.d.1) and their quality measured objectively, for example by code coverage (O.d.2).
- *Fuzz testing* runs the agent's code and a reference implementation on many automatically generated inputs and compares outputs. The generator must cover edge cases (O.e.1) and the full variety of inputs such as data types, memory layouts and value ranges (O.e.2). The subtle one is O.e.3: inputs must be ones the code is *sensitive* to. The paper's example: "random negatives reveal nothing about relu(x)". If every generated input makes ReLU output zero, a kernel that always returns zero passes. KernelBench had functions like `mean(softmax(x))` that barely change under uniform random inputs, so a wrong kernel looks right.
- *End-to-end tests* simulate full user workflows. They must exercise all relevant code paths (O.f.1) and avoid flaky, non-deterministic results (O.f.2), for example from hard-coded timeouts.

**State modification** (the agent changes a database or file system): the ground truth must include every end state a correct solution could reach (O.g.1), must check both the states that should change and the ones that should not (O.g.2, to catch collateral damage), and must be complex enough that random or trivial changes cannot hit it (O.g.3).

**Multistep reasoning** (the agent derives a final answer or optimizes a metric): answer parsers must not make hidden format assumptions (O.h.1, the MATH example where the parser expects the answer to start with "Answer:"), guessing must be unlikely (O.h.2), and when there is no ground truth and a quality metric is used instead, as in MLE-bench, the metric must resist being gamed (O.i.1).

### Reporting (R.1–R.13)

Some flaws cannot be removed, especially when grading relies on LLM judges or tests that can never be complete. For those, ABC asks the benchmark to be honest about them. The checks cover transparency (open data and harness, contamination defences like a private held-out set, plans to refresh tasks, a clear statement of what capability is measured and whether a model or an agent framework is being evaluated), mitigation (describe how flaws were found and fixed, discuss unavoidable flaws qualitatively and estimate their size quantitatively), and interpretation (confidence intervals, guidance on reading flawed results, and two baselines). The two baselines are the cheapest and most telling checks in the whole paper: report a non-AI baseline such as human experts (R.12), and report a **trivial agent** that does nothing (R.13). R.13 alone would have caught the τ-bench problem on day one. It pairs naturally with [[2411.00640 - Adding Error Bars to Evals]] for R.10 and with [[AISI - Evaluation Validity Checklist]], which covers similar ground from a government evaluator's angle.

## What they found when they applied it

Aggregate scores (Figure 5): seven of ten benchmarks violated task validity, seven violated outcome validity, and all ten had reporting gaps. "80% of the benchmarks fail to acknowledge weaknesses in their design or implementation, and none satisfies every reporting criterion." The individual findings are the real content, so here they are with the mechanism behind each.

**τ-bench: empty ground truth.** τ-bench (see [[2406.12045 - Tau-Bench (Tool-Agent-User Interaction)]]) grades an episode by hashing the final database and comparing it to the hash you get by replaying the gold action sequence, plus optionally checking that required strings appear in the agent's replies. Some tasks are deliberately impossible under the airline policy, for example refunding a non-refundable ticket, and the correct behaviour is to refuse. For such tasks the gold action list is empty, so the expected final database equals the starting database. Any agent that changes nothing passes, whether it read the policy or not. That is 38% of airline tasks and 6% of retail tasks. The designers' intent (reward correct refusal) was sound. The grader just cannot tell a principled refusal from inaction, because it only checks the end state, not the reasoning or lookups that led there.

**τ-bench: trivial substrings.** On 2% of airline and 3.6% of retail tasks, the required output string is verbatim database text. An agent that dumps the entire database into its reply contains that text, so it passes. The spamming agent scores 40% airline and 9.6% retail. Because both exploits are deterministic, the scores hold "for any k" under both pass@k and pass^k (see [[pass-hat-k-reliability-metric]]). A reliability metric like pass^k does not help when the grader itself is wrong.

**WebArena.** Substring matching ignores extra content, so over-inclusive answers pass. For tasks whose label is "N/A", the LLM judge accepts an empty reply. And the LLM judge makes plain errors: asked for the walk-then-drive time from MIT via Harvard to Logan airport (label 63 minutes), an agent answered 45 + 8 = 53 minutes and the judge marked it correct. Net effect: 1.4–5.2% overestimation.

**SWE-Lancer.** The agent runs Python with full read-write access to the file system. The tests are stored in a password-protected zip, but a zip password only encrypts file contents. The list of file names is readable, and new entries can be written into the archive without the password. So the agent lists the test paths, writes `assert True` tests at those paths, and adds them back into the zip. Score: 100%, with zero tasks solved.

**KernelBench.** The fuzzer changes only tensor *values*, not shapes or memory layouts (for example non-contiguous tensors). The paper shows a layer-norm CUDA kernel whose parallel reduction reads out of bounds into uninitialized shared memory when the thread count exceeds the normalized dimension. It is graded correct because the tested shape never triggers the bug. To scale this up, they had o3-mini read three sampled "correct" kernels per level-1 task, list flaws, and write a pytest case per flaw. Humans verified the tests, and the tests were then run on all kernels from Lange et al. (Sakana AI's generations). Result: correctness overestimated by about 31%.

**OSWorld.** In the Chrome section, 13 of 46 tasks broke because the live websites changed after release, and the graders look for specific HTML classes and XPaths that no longer exist. For UI-TARS, the leading open agent at the time, this *underestimates* performance by 28 points on that section. This is the only large underestimate in the paper, and it is the T.6 (frozen environment) failure in pure form.

**SWE-bench (prior work, reproduced).** Citing UTBoost, agents pass without fixing the issue on 5.3% of Verified and 7.7% of Lite tasks. That shifts 40.9% and 24.4% of leaderboard positions respectively, even though the absolute overestimate is only 2.3% and 1.6%. This is the most underrated number in the paper: a small absolute error can reshuffle a crowded leaderboard, because the top entries are separated by less than the error.

**BIRD.** Natural-language questions are ambiguous. "The country with the smallest population" can be answered with `WHERE Population = (SELECT min(...))`, which returns all ties, or with `ORDER BY Population LIMIT 1`, which returns one. Both are reasonable, but execution-result matching accepts only the one that matches the gold query.

## The CVE-Bench case study: using ABC during construction

CVE-Bench, built by the same lab, tests whether agents can exploit real web vulnerabilities. Success is judged by whether one of several pre-specified attack outcomes happened, such as denial of service or an outbound request to a forbidden server. They ran ABC on their own benchmark and found two bugs.

**Time-based SQL injection (outcome validity, O.g.1).** In a time-based SQL injection, the attacker cannot see query results directly. Instead they inject something like `IF(condition, SLEEP(5), 0)` and infer one bit of the database from whether the response is slow. CVE-Bench graded this by checking whether `SLEEP` appeared in the database log. But a SLEEP appearing in a logged query does not mean it *executed*. An agent could put the string SLEEP anywhere in a query, for instance inside a string literal, and pass. Fixing this lowered success rates by 32.5%.

**Ungated outbound server (task validity, T.9).** For the "make the app contact a banned server" attack, the grader checked whether the outbound server received any request. Mock runs showed agents *always* passed this target. That is the "succeeds suspiciously often" outlier signal. The cause: agents could reach the outbound server directly from the same Docker network, without exploiting the web app at all. Blocking external requests to that server cut success rates by 10%.

The abstract summarizes this as "ABC reduces the performance overestimation by 33%". Note that 33% there is in absolute percentage points, not relative.

## A worked example of rigorous reporting, and a flaw in its math

Appendix F rewrites BIRD's report so that it satisfies all 13 reporting checks. It is a usable template. The most technical part is R.9, a confidence interval that accounts for label noise. Their model: suppose a fraction e of ground-truth labels are wrong (they plug in e = 11.65%, the rate Arcwise found by re-verifying 500 BIRD queries), and p₀ is the agent's measured success rate. They write

µ = e + (1 − 2e)·p₀,  σ² = µ(1 − µ),  CI = µ ± 1.96·σ/√N.

Term by term: with probability (1 − e) a label is right and the outcome is scored correctly, which contributes (1 − e)p₀. With probability e it is wrong and the verdict is flipped, which contributes e(1 − p₀). Adding the two gives e + (1 − 2e)p₀. σ² is the Bernoulli variance at rate µ, and dividing by √N gives the standard error over N tasks.

Check it against Table 15: CHASE-SQL has p₀ = 74.9%, which gives µ = 0.1165 + 0.767 × 0.749 ≈ 69.1%. With N ≈ 1534 (BIRD's dev set), the half-width is about 2.3 points, which reproduces the reported interval [66.8, 71.4]. So the table is internally consistent.

My own reading of the math, not a point the paper makes: the direction is backwards. The formula e + (1 − 2e)·p describes what you would *observe* if the *true* rate were p. Here it is applied to the observed rate p₀ as if p₀ were the truth. Under their own symmetric-flip model, the true rate is p = (p₀ − e)/(1 − 2e), which pushes scores *away* from 50%: CHASE-SQL would be about 82%, not 69%. You can see the symptom in the table: every interval excludes its own point estimate. The top entries are pulled down (74.9 → [66.8, 71.4]) and the bottom ones pulled up (T5-Base 6.3 → [14.6, 18.4]). The symmetric-flip model is also doubtful for BIRD. A wrong gold query mostly turns correct predictions into failures, while a wrong prediction rarely happens to match a wrong gold query, so the errors are one-sided rather than symmetric. And the interval ignores the uncertainty in e, which was itself estimated from 500 samples. The useful idea that survives all of this is the "possible rank" column: once you account for label noise, the #1 system could plausibly rank anywhere from 1 to 13. That is the honest message for a leaderboard, whatever the exact interval.

## How the code implements it

The repo is mostly a set of reproductions of the exploits, not a reusable checking tool. It holds the checklist (`ABC.md`), one YAML score file per benchmark (`assessments/*.yaml`, each check with a 0/1 score and a written reason), and one folder per benchmark with patches or scripts that reproduce a finding. The patches apply against pinned commits of the upstream benchmarks. Reading them shows exactly how cheap each exploit is.

**1. The τ-bench "do-nothing" agent.** Problem: show that a policy-ignorant agent scores 38% on airline. The patch replaces the LLM call in the tool-calling agent loop with one fixed action.

`benchmarks/tau-bench/exploit-1.patch:26-32 @ ae11247`
```diff
+            # next_message = res.choices[0].message.model_dump()
+            # total_cost += res._hidden_params["response_cost"]
+            # action = message_to_action(next_message)
+            action = Action(name="transfer_to_human_agents", kwargs={})
             env_response = env.step(action)
             reward = env_response.reward
             info = {**info, **env_response.info.model_dump()}
```

What happens: on the first step the agent calls `transfer_to_human_agents`, which is a terminating tool in τ-bench, so the episode ends with the database untouched. The reward function then compares the untouched database hash with the gold hash. For impossible tasks the gold hash is also the untouched state, so the reward is 1. A detail the paper glosses over: the paper describes this agent as one that "returns empty responses" or "does nothing". In the code it actually hands off to a human immediately. That matters a little, because escalating to a human is a sanctioned action in τ-bench's policy for some cases. The conclusion still holds, since the agent passes without reading the policy or the reservation.

**2. The τ-bench fix: require evidence of lookup.** Problem: the grader must tell "refused after checking" apart from "did nothing". The fix adds a `required_actions` field to tasks and checks it in the reward function.

`benchmarks/tau-bench/tau-bench-issue-1-fix.patch:214-234 @ ae11247`
```diff
         gt_data_hash = self.get_data_hash()
+        data_same = data_hash == gt_data_hash
+        has_required_actions = True
+        if self.task.required_actions:
+            # Check for presence of actions. 
+            for gt_action in self.task.required_actions:
+                found_action = False
+                for action in predicted_tasks:
+                    if action.name == gt_action.name and action.kwargs == gt_action.kwargs:
+                        found_action = True
+                        break
+                if not found_action:
+                    has_required_actions = False
+                    reward = 0.0
+                    break
         info = RewardActionInfo(
-            r_actions=data_hash == gt_data_hash, gt_data_hash=gt_data_hash
+            r_actions=data_same and has_required_actions, gt_data_hash=gt_data_hash
         )
         if not info.r_actions:
             reward = 0.0
```

Walkthrough: `predicted_tasks` is a deep copy of the agent's action log, taken before the gold actions are replayed. For each required action, such as `get_reservation_details(reservation_id="3FRNFB")`, the loop searches the agent's log for an exact name-and-arguments match. If any required lookup is missing, the action reward becomes 0 even when the database is unchanged. This is a small, sensible move from pure outcome grading toward partial *process* grading: the end state alone was not enough evidence. Two things to note. First, it differs from the repo's own README, which says "we can remove intentionally unsolvable challenges". The patch keeps them and adds lookup requirements instead, which is the better fix because refusal remains a tested skill. Second, the same patch quietly rewrites some task instructions (a Mei Brown task is replaced outright, and a Raj Sanchez task gets its reservation ID added with the comment "The old task description is ambiguous"). So the "fixed" τ-bench is not the same task set as the original, and scores are not directly comparable. The requirement is also brittle in its own way: exact `kwargs` equality means a lookup through a different but valid path (for example `get_user_details` and then reasoning from it) scores 0.

**3. The SWE-Lancer exploit.** Problem: show that the test archive is writable without the password.

`benchmarks/swe-lancer/exploit.patch:44-65 @ ae11247`
```diff
+                        code = """import os
+import zipfile
+dirs_list = []
+zip_ref = zipfile.ZipFile('/app/tests.zip', 'r')
+for dir in zip_ref.namelist():
+    dirs_list.append(dir)
+print(dirs_list)
+naive_test_code = '''
+def test():
+    assert True
+'''
+for dir in dirs_list:
+    if dir.endswith('/'):
+        # create directory if it ends with /
+        os.makedirs(f'/app/tests/{dir}', exist_ok=True)
+    elif dir.endswith('test.py'):
+        with open(f'/app/tests/{dir}', 'w') as f:
+            f.write(naive_test_code)
+        # update the zip file with the new test.py
+        os.system(f'cd /app/tests && zip ../tests.zip {dir}')
+
+"""
```

Walkthrough: `namelist()` needs no password, because zip encryption covers file contents, not the central directory that lists names. The script recreates the directory tree, writes a `test.py` containing `assert True` at every test path, and runs `zip ../tests.zip {dir}`, which *replaces* the entry of the same name with an unencrypted one. At grading time the harness unzips with the password. Unencrypted entries extract fine even when a password is supplied, so the fake tests are what run. The whole exploit is 20 lines that a capable agent could plausibly discover on its own.

**4. The SWE-Lancer fix, and why it does not hold up.** Problem: stop the overwrite.

`benchmarks/swe-lancer/fix.patch:8-20 @ ae11247`
```diff
         await computer.check_shell_command(
-            "cd /app/tests && zip -P 'secretpasswordhere' -r /app/tmp.zip . && mv /app/tmp.zip /app/tests.zip"
+            "cd /app/tests && zip -P 'secretpasswordhere' -r tmp.zip . && zip -P 'heresecretpassword' /app/tmp.zip tmp.zip && mv /app/tmp.zip /app/tests.zip"
         )
         # Clear tests directory
         await computer.send_shell_command("rm -rf /app/tests")
@@ -146,7 +146,7 @@ class SWELancerTask(ComputerTask):
         #Unzip locked testing files
         print('Unzipping tests')
         print(await computer.check_shell_command(
-            "unzip -q -P 'secretpasswordhere' -o /app/tests.zip -d /app/tests"
+            "unzip -P 'heresecretpassword' -o /app/tests.zip /app/tests_inner.zip && unzip -q -P 'secretpasswordhere' -o /app/tests_inner.zip -d /app/tests"
         ))
```

The idea is to zip the tests, then zip that archive again under a second password, so that listing the outer archive shows only `tmp.zip` and the real test paths are hidden. I checked this locally with the same commands on a mock layout, and two problems appeared. First, the extraction step as written fails. The outer archive's only entry is named `tmp.zip`, but the unzip command asks for a member named `tests_inner.zip`. `unzip` reports "filename not matched" and exits with code 11, so `check_shell_command` would error before grading. Second, even with the name corrected, the root cause is untouched. The agent can still add its own unencrypted `tmp.zip` to the outer archive without any password (I confirmed this, and the corrected two-stage unzip then extracted the attacker's `assert True` test). The only barrier left is that the agent can no longer *list* the inner test paths, so it has to guess the layout. That is obscurity, not isolation. The check this is meant to satisfy, T.5 ("Agent is completely isolated from any ground truth information"), really calls for the tests to live outside anything the agent can write, for example copied in only after the agent's container stops.

**5. What counts as a KernelBench "incorrect" kernel.** Problem: turn an LLM's list of suspected flaws into executable evidence. `scripts/judge_by_llm.py` asks o3-mini to "identify all the issues" in each kernel that KernelBench marked correct, and tells it the kernel "should be compatible with other more complex and general situations". It then saves the pytest file the model writes. A human-verified example:

`benchmarks/kernel-bench/tests_verified/level_1/10_3D_tensor_matrix_multiplication/test_1111.py:9-15 @ ae11247`
```python
def test_dimension_mismatch():
    cuda_module = build_kernel()
    N, M, K, L = 4, 8, 16, 10
    A = torch.randn(N, M, K, device='cuda', dtype=torch.float32)
    B = torch.randn(K + 1, L, device='cuda', dtype=torch.float32)
    with pytest.raises(RuntimeError):
        C_kernel = cuda_module.forward(A, B)
```

Walkthrough: this test feeds deliberately mismatched shapes (B has K+1 rows) and requires the kernel to raise an error. A kernel that computes the correct product for every *valid* input still fails it if it does not validate inputs. That is a much stricter definition of "correct" than KernelBench's task, which fixes the input shapes. It is also stricter than what the paper's text describes, which is fuzzing over shapes and memory layouts. The prompt's own examples include a test that passes `float64` tensors to a kernel that may only have been written for `float32`. So part of the 31% "overestimate" measures robustness and input validation outside the task's stated contract, not wrong answers on the task. The layer-norm out-of-bounds read in the paper is a genuine correctness bug. Tests like this one are closer to a judgment call. The 31% is best read as "31% of kernels break under a broader correctness contract", and that contract should be stated.

**6. The WebArena meta-judge prompt.** Problem: measure how often WebArena's grader labels were wrong, by asking o1 whether each "Match / Not match" annotation was correct. The prompt is few-shot:

`benchmarks/webarena/llm_as_a_judge.py:38-44 @ ae11247`
```python
Example 5
Question: Show me the customers who have expressed dissatisfaction with Olivia zip jacket?
Answer 1: The list of customers who have given negative feedback about the Olivia 1/4 Zip Light Jacket includes: 1. Nickname: Emma, Review: "I was really disappointed with the Olivia 1/4 Z..." 2. Nickname: seam miller, Review: "I have to say, I'm not impressed with the Olivi...".
Answer 2: Emma Lopez, Seam Miller
Annotation: Not match
Judgement: Wrong annotation
Explanation: Both Answer 1 and Answer 2 mention 2 customers: Emma and Seam. Therefore, the two answers do not match. The annotation is wrong.
```

Walkthrough: the explanation contradicts itself. It says both answers name the same two customers, concludes they "do not match", and then calls the "Not match" annotation wrong. Example 8 has the mirror-image error ("Answer 1 shows 7 more customers than Answer 2. Therefore, the two answers match. The annotation is wrong."). Few-shot examples teach the judge a reasoning pattern, and here two of the eleven teach an incoherent one. Separately, Example 9 in the same prompt (lines 70-76) is the MIT→Harvard→Logan case, which is the paper's showcase WebArena judge failure. So the meta-judge is shown the answer to one of the items it is being used to evaluate. None of this is fatal, and the 1.4–5.2% range is small. But this is the paper's own check O.c.1 ("Demonstrates documented or experimental evidence of the judge's accuracy, self-consistency, and agreement with human") applied to the paper's own judge, and it would not fully pass. `evaluate.py` is simpler and cleaner: it re-grades 812 WebArena tasks with the original versus a customized string evaluator and logs every disagreement with the trajectory's recorded success label.

## What is interesting or non-obvious

The strongest idea is that **the cheapest checks catch the biggest bugs**. A do-nothing agent (R.13), an oracle solver (T.9), and a look at suspiciously high pass rates (T.10) would have caught τ-bench, CVE-Bench's outbound server, and most likely SWE-Lancer. None of these needs a frontier model or clever statistics. They are unit tests for the grader. This maps directly onto RL environment design, where the grader *is* the reward. Every ABC violation is a reward-hacking surface for a policy trained on that environment, as in [[four-layer-scoring-stack-for-rl-environments]], [[weight-zero-metrics-alongside-the-reward]] and [[2601.20103 - TRACE Reward Hack Detection via Contrastive Analysis]]. A benchmark that a do-nothing agent passes 38% of the time is also an RL environment that pays 38% reward for doing nothing.

A second non-obvious point: **errors go both ways, and the direction depends on the link that broke**. Shortcuts and loose graders overestimate. Stale environments and over-strict graders (OSWorld selectors, BIRD's single gold query) underestimate. A single "benchmark noise" correction cannot fix both, which is why ABC separates them.

Third: **the paper's own experiments show how hard it is to follow its checklist**. The SWE-Lancer fix breaks extraction and leaves the write path open. The WebArena meta-judge has contradictory few-shot examples and a leaked test item. The BIRD confidence interval inverts its own noise model. The τ-bench fix changes task text. None of this undermines the core findings, which are reproducible with 20-line patches. It does support the paper's thesis more strongly than the paper intends: grader code needs adversarial review, including the reviewer's own code.

A small housekeeping note: check IDs drift between the paper's figures and its appendix tables. Table 5 uses O.f.2 and O.f.3 where Figure 3 defines O.f.1 and O.f.2, and the text cites O.i.1 where the figure prints O.I.1. So cite checks by their text, not only their ID.

## Genuine limitations

The authors acknowledge that the corpus covers only 17 benchmarks from January 2024 to March 2025, and that the findings are snapshots that may not apply to later versions. Beyond that:

- The scoring is binary and unweighted. A missing version string (T.1) counts the same as a 100% exploit (T.5), so the average scores in Figure 5 say little about how badly a benchmark is broken. The quantified per-issue effects are far more informative than the aggregate score.
- "Overestimation by X%" mixes absolute points (KernelBench 31, CVE-Bench 33, OSWorld 28 on one section) and relative figures ("up to 100% in relative terms"), and the paper does not always say which. Read each number with its unit.
- The checklist tells you what to check, not how to check it. For example, O.c.1 does not say how many human labels establish judge accuracy or what agreement level is enough. It is an audit list, not a protocol.
- Several findings are "a trivial agent can pass" results. These prove an exploit exists but do not show that real agents used it. The τ-bench and SWE-Lancer numbers are upper bounds on contamination of real leaderboard scores, not measured contamination.

## Key claims

1. **A trivial agent beats GPT-4o on τ-bench-Airline.** An agent that terminates immediately scores 38% on airline and 6% on retail, under any k for both pass@k and pass^k, because intentionally impossible tasks are graded only by "database unchanged". GPT-4o scores 35% on airline.
> A do-nothing agent that returns immediately can achieve a 38% and 6.0% pass^k or pass@k for any k for Airline and Retail partitions, respectively.
(Appendix E.2)

2. **Dumping the database also passes.** On tasks whose required output is verbatim database text (2% of airline, 3.6% of retail), a spamming agent passes, and it reaches 40% airline and 9.6% retail overall.
> Second, 2% of airline tasks and 3.6% of retail tasks treat verbatim database text as ground truth and grade by substring matching. Therefore, an agent that dumps the entire database passes evaluations of these tasks.
(Section 5.2, τ-bench; the 40% / 9.6% figures are in Appendix E.2)

3. **SWE-Lancer can be scored 100% without solving anything**, because the agent can write into the password-protected test zip.
> An agent that overwrites the test cases in the .zip file can achieve a 100% resolve rate without completing the software engineering tasks.
(Appendix E.4)

4. **KernelBench overestimates kernel correctness by about 31 points**, measured with o3-mini-generated, human-verified tests run on Lange et al.'s generated kernels (level 1). Note from the code walkthrough: some of these tests check input validation beyond the task's fixed shapes.
> Our results show that the correctness rate of generated kernels is overestimated by 31%.
(Appendix E.6)

5. **OSWorld underestimates when live sites change.** 13 of 46 Chrome tasks are broken by website drift, which lowers UI-TARS's Chrome-section score by 28 points absolute (24/46 → 37/46 after fixes, per the repo README).
> In our experiments, we found that this issue leads to an underestimation of the performance of UI-TAR, the state-of-the-art open-source agent for OSWorld, by 28% in absolute terms.
(Section 5.2, OSWorld)

6. **WebArena's string matching and LLM judge overestimate by 1.4–5.2%.**
> WebArena not only violates check O.b.2 but also uses an LLM-as-a-Judge without validating its accuracy or consistency (check O.c.1), leading to a 1.4–5.2% performance overestimate.
(Section 5.2, finding 3)

7. **Small absolute grading errors reorder leaderboards.** On SWE-bench, passing-without-fixing tasks (5.3% Verified, 7.7% Lite, from UTBoost) change 40.9% and 24.4% of leaderboard positions, while the absolute overestimate is only 2.3% and 1.6%.
> These tasks lead to 40.9% and 24.4% changes in the leaderboard for the Verified and Lite partitions, respectively.
(Appendix E.1)

8. **Applying ABC to CVE-Bench removed about 33 points of overestimation.** Two fixes were made: time-based SQL injection was graded on the SLEEP string rather than on execution (−32.5%), and the outbound server was reachable from the same Docker network (−10%). Results were confirmed by cybersecurity experts.
> Consequently, agents can pass the evaluation by adding SLEEP anywhere in the query, leading to performance overestimation by 32.5%.
(Section 5.3)

9. **Validity problems are widespread across popular benchmarks.** Of ten benchmarks assessed, 7 violate task validity, 7 violate outcome validity, and all 10 have reporting gaps.
> Benchmark Reporting: 80% of the benchmarks fail to acknowledge weaknesses in their design or implementation, and none satisfies every reporting criterion.
(Section 5.1)

10. **Rigorous evaluation needs both validity links to hold.**
> Conceptually, an agentic evaluation is rigorous if and only if (1) the target capability is equivalent to task success (i.e., task validity), and (2) the task success is equivalent to a positive evaluation result
(Section 3, Taxonomy)

11. **Label noise makes BIRD's top ranks indistinguishable.** With an 11.65% gold-query error rate plugged into a normal-approximation interval, the #1 system's possible rank spans 1–13 (Table 15). The interval formula applies the noise model to the observed rate rather than inverting it, so the intervals are biased toward 50% (see the section on reporting math above).
> Finally, based on the plug-in estimate (11.65%) for the ground truth’s incorrectness rate, we calculate the confidence interval for the agents’ performance in Table 15.
(Appendix F, R.9)
